web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
question: What growth rate does $64.53 price in, and does an unbiased SOTP justify risking capital after Pass 1's watch flags?

epigraph.quote: A cheap headline multiple only stays cheap when segment margins expand, stock-based pay is contained, and peers are not outspending you four-to-one on R&D.
epigraph.author: Institutional Research Desk

web_blocks.html: At the November 20, 2026 close of $64.53, DFIN carries a $1.57 billion market cap and a $1.68 billion Finviz enterprise value [30, 45]. Basic shares stand at 24.50 million, with 22.75 million in the float and 25.0 million Q3 diluted shares [30, 45]. Using September 30, 2026 net debt of $99.8 million ($127.0 million debt minus $27.2 million cash), implied EV sits near $1.67 billion [45, 46]. Shares trade at 17.01x trailing GAAP P/E ($3.79 TTM EPS) and 11.43x forward P/E (~$5.65 forward EPS), giving a 0.86 PEG ratio on 13.22% projected five-year EPS growth [30]. On cash flow and sales, DFIN trades at 7.46x EV/EBITDA, 2.13x EV/Sales, 2.00x Price/Sales, 3.86x Price/Book, and 8.78x P/FCF [30]. Normalized against FY2025 FCF ($107.8 million) and Q4 guidance, shares trade near ~14.6x normalized FCF and sit 14.3% below the $75.33 sell-side consensus target [15, 30, 46].

A Reverse DCF shows what $64.53 already prices in. Starting from a $1.68 billion EV and $787.2 million trailing sales, we apply a 9.5% WACC (0.68 beta, 0.33x debt/equity) and a 2.5% terminal growth rate [15, 30]. We model normalized FCF at 14.5% of sales (~$114 million initial FCF), which reflects ~$55–$60 million annual software CapEx and $34.3 million in trailing stock-based compensation (SBC) [15, 46]. Under those inputs, $64.53 requires only 2.5% to 3.5% annual consolidated sales growth over ten years, reaching ~$155 million in normalized Year 10 FCF. Investors are not pricing in collapse. They are pricing in muted growth because print runoff, deal cyclicality, and segment margin cracks cap software multiple expansion [45, 46].

Pass 1's blind-spot audit forces a sharp downward reset to our Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) fair value. Earlier optimism assumed Arc Suite would compound at mid-teens rates alongside ActiveDisclosure, earning Software Solutions a 4.25x EV/Sales premium above Workiva. Q3 2026 filings disproved both premises [45, 53]. First, IC-SS (Arc Suite) fell -1.9% YoY in Q3 ($31.1 million) and posted 0.0% organic growth across 9M 2026 ($97.9 million) post-TSR [45]. Second, CM-SS Segment Adjusted EBITDA declined -6.8% YoY in Q3 to $19.2 million (-490 bps to 30.0% margin) as SG&A jumped +22.4% [45]. Third, Workiva ($1.041B–$1.044B FY26 guide, +17% YoY, 110% net retention) turned GAAP profitable while spending $167.7 million on 9M R&D—over 4.5x DFIN's entire $36.3 million 9M CapEx [45, 53, 54]. An honest Software multiple for DFIN must sit near Workiva (~3.5x–3.7x), not at a premium. We model FY2027E Software Solutions at $405 million (+6.5% growth) and apply 3.60x EV/Sales ($1,458 million EV).

web_blocks.if_off: If ActiveDisclosure slows below 15% YoY or SEC e-delivery rules cut IC-CCM faster than 8% yearly, base fair value falls toward $60–$64. Conversely, if CM-SS margins recover above 34% and Arc Suite resumes growth, fair value can expand toward $85–$88.

web_blocks.html: Valuation Re-Underwriting Trigger: Base fair value moves back toward $85–$88 only if CM-SS Segment Adjusted EBITDA margin rebounds above 34%, IC-SS resumes positive organic growth, and quarterly share buybacks outpace $8.5M/quarter SBC. Conversely, an SEC e-delivery mandate or ActiveDisclosure slowdown below 15% pushes fair value toward $60.

book_paragraphs: Now that Chapters 1 through 6 have audited Donnelley Financial Solutions without looking at its stock chart, we open the live November 20, 2026 valuation ledger. At a closing price of $64.53, DFIN carries an equity market capitalization of $1.57 billion across 24.50 million basic shares, and a Finviz enterprise value of $1.68 billion. On headline multiples, the stock looks optically cheap: 17.01 times trailing GAAP earnings, 11.43 times forward earnings, 7.46 times EV-to-EBITDA, and 8.78 times trailing free cash flow.

Yet a disciplined analyst never stops at a low trailing multiple without asking why the market put it on sale. In our refreshed Pass 1 audit, we uncovered six concrete reasons why Wall Street is cautious. First, Arc Suite in Investment Companies Software stalled, slipping 1.9% year-over-year in Q3 2026 and posting flat zero-percent organic growth over nine months once the Tailored Shareholder Reports rollout lapped. Second, Capital Markets Software saw Segment Adjusted EBITDA drop 6.8% in Q3, compressing its margin by 490 basis points to 30.0% as SG&A surged 22.4% and bad-debt provisions climbed.

Third, competitive pressure is intensifying. Direct rival Workiva crossed a billion-dollar revenue run-rate in Q3 2026 with 17% growth, turned GAAP profitable, and spent $167.7 million on nine-month R&D—more than four and a half times DFIN's entire nine-month capital spending of $36.3 million. Meanwhile, SS&C Intralinks and Datasite are rolling out agentic and generative AI across Virtual Data Rooms. Fourth, the SEC's 2026 deregulatory rulemaking agenda threatens Form N-PORT reporting and proposes replacing paper-by-default rules with electronic delivery, directly endangering DFIN's $109.4 million trailing Print and Distribution revenue.

Fifth, balance-sheet footnotes remind us that $405.5 million of goodwill makes up over half of total assets, $23.3 million of residual frozen pension liabilities remain despite the 2025 settlement, and trailing stock-based compensation jumped 30.4% to $34.3 million while Q3 buybacks slowed to just $6.9 million. Sixth, five senior executives—including CEO Daniel Leib, CFO David Gardella, and departing Global Capital Markets President Craig Clay—sold 201,650 shares in early November 2026, mostly outside automatic 10b5-1 trading plans.

Let's see what those realities mean for intrinsic value using both a Reverse DCF and an unbiased Sum-of-the-Parts valuation. On a Reverse DCF at $64.53—using a 9.5% discount rate, 2.5% terminal growth, and normalized free cash flow margins of 14.5% (~$114 million baseline)—the market is pricing in roughly 2.5% to 3.5% annual revenue growth over ten years. That is a low bar, which explains why the downside in a benign economy is cushioned near $50.

However, on Sum-of-the-Parts, we cannot award DFIN's Software Solutions segment a higher sales multiple than faster-growing, GAAP-profitable Workiva. Valuing $405 million of FY2027E Software Solutions revenue at a realistic 3.60 times EV-to-Sales ($1,458 million) and $88 million of legacy Compliance and Communications EBITDA at 4.75 times ($418 million), subtracting $65 million for corporate drag and $50 million for remaining net debt and pension obligations after 18 months of cash generation, gives $1,761 million of equity value. Divided across 23.8 million diluted shares—reflecting slower net buybacks due to $34.3 million in annual stock compensation—our re-underwritten Base Fair Value lands at $74.00 per share, virtually identical to the $75.33 Wall Street consensus.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Unbiased Re-Underwriting Matters
book_callouts.text: When new filings show Arc Suite flattening, CM-SS margins dropping 490 bps, and SBC rising above buybacks, an honest analyst lowers the Sum-of-the-Parts multiple rather than clinging to stale $92 targets. Our $74.00 Base Fair Value matches Wall Street consensus ($75.33) and forces us to test whether $64.53 still offers enough margin of safety.

book_subsections.title: 7A. Reverse DCF Check: Low Growth Priced In, Low Margin for Error
paragraphs: Starting from DFIN's $1.68 billion enterprise value and $787.2 million of trailing revenue, a Reverse DCF solves for the top-line pace needed to earn a 9.5% annual hurdle rate. Normalized free cash flow runs near 14.5% of sales, or roughly $114 million per year once working-capital timing swings settle and $55 million to $60 million of annual software capital spending is funded.

At that baseline, DFIN only needs to compound revenue at 2.5% to 3.5% annually over the next decade to justify $64.53. Yet look at why the market refuses to pay more: consolidated nine-month 2026 revenue grew just 3.4%, Asia fell 32.5% from 2023 to 2025, and electronic-delivery rulemaking could accelerate print declines beyond 8% a year.

Even more telling is the quality of cash flow relative to capitalized software. While DFIN reported $131.0 million in nine-month free cash flow, $41.2 million of capitalized software amortization sits above the operating line while $36.3 million of CapEx sits in investing cash flows. Meanwhile, trailing twelve-month stock compensation of $34.3 million is treated as a non-cash add-back in operating cash flow, meaning real free cash flow after stock compensation dilution runs closer to $75 million to $90 million on a steady-state annual basis.

book_subsections.title: 7B. Why DFIN Software Cannot Earn a Premium Multiple to Workiva
paragraphs: In earlier cycles, bulls argued DFIN's software segment deserved more than 4.25 times sales. Comparing Q3 2026 SEC filings directly against Workiva exposes why that argument fails today. Workiva grew Q3 revenue 17% to $263 million, guided full-year 2026 revenue above $1.04 billion, achieved 110% net dollar retention, crossed into GAAP operating profitability, and spent $167.7 million on nine-month R&D.

By contrast, roughly a third of DFIN's software revenue sits in Investment Companies (Arc Suite), which contracted 1.9% in Q3, and another big slice sits in transactional Venue data rooms tied to cyclical M&A deal counts. Awarding 3.60 times FY2027E sales ($1,458 million) to DFIN Software is already generous until ActiveDisclosure's 24% growth is matched by margin recovery and Arc Suite re-acceleration.

Comparing DFIN against our live November 20 snapshot peers reinforces the same discipline. AvePoint (AVPT) trades at $16.49 with +23.74% TTM revenue growth, 80% pure SaaS mix, and zero funded debt. Moody's (MCO) commands 45.88% operating margins and 79.81% ROE on recurring credit and analytics data. Microsoft (MSFT) compounds at 17.91% top-line growth with 47.1% operating margins. Even though DFIN carries the lowest headline P/E at 17.01x, its +4.85% trailing top-line growth and cyclical legacy tail explain why institutional capital prefers cleaner software compounders.

book_subsections.title: 7C. The SBC Dilution vs. Buyback Reality Check
paragraphs: A subtle leak in DFIN's per-share compounding math surfaced in Q3 2026. Trailing twelve-month stock-based compensation jumped 30.4% year-over-year to $34.3 million, including $7.5 million in Q3 alone. Meanwhile, share repurchases slowed sharply to just $6.9 million (146,672 shares) in Q3 2026, down from $35.5 million in Q3 2025.

When quarterly buybacks fall below quarterly stock compensation, share count stops shrinking rapidly. Under DFIN's 2026 proxy Annual Incentive Plan, 50% of annual executive bonuses tie to Non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA—which excludes stock-based compensation—and 30% tie to Software Solutions net sales growth. That formula rewards top-line software mix and Adjusted EBITDA even when stock grants rise and CM-SS segment margins fall 490 basis points. Modeling diluted shares holding near 23.8 million through FY2027—rather than shrinking aggressively to 23.2 million—further trims per-share fair value down to $74.00.

book_subsections.title: 7D. Stress-Testing the $50.00 Bear Case and $88.00 Bull Case
paragraphs: In our $50.00 Bear Case (25% probability), an IPO and M&A freeze combines with accelerated SEC e-delivery rules, trimming CCM EBITDA to $82 million at 3.50 times ($287 million) and compressing Software to 2.80 times $390 million ($1,092 million). Subtracting $75 million for corporate drag and $79 million in net debt and pension claims across 24.5 million shares yields $50.00.

In our $88.00 Bull Case (20% probability), IPO activity thaws, CM-SS margins rebound past 34%, and Software earns 4.15 times $410 million ($1,701.5 million) alongside 5.25 times CCM EBITDA ($483 million). That bridges to $88.00, still well below $92.00 because of Workiva's R&D lead and executive selling overhangs.

Look at our Sum-of-the-Parts sensitivity matrix across 3.00x to 4.15x Software EV-to-Sales and 3.75x to 5.25x CCM EBITDA. Across the realistic central band of 3.00x to 3.60x Software sales, DFIN's intrinsic value clusters tightly between $60.08 and $75.84 per share. Only if the market awards DFIN Software over 4.15x sales—a multiple higher than GAAP-profitable Workiva—does fair value cross $83. Next, Chapter 8 examines whether the live chart gives us any technical edge to bridge that modest 14.7% base upside.

book_subsections.title: 7E. Reconciling Wall Street Consensus ($75.33) With Unbiased SOTP ($74.00)
paragraphs: One of the strongest sanity checks on any re-underwritten valuation model is comparing it against sell-side consensus without blindly copying it. In the November 20 Finviz ledger, consensus analyst targets sit at $75.33—within two percent of our independent $74.00 Base Case. Why did our prior November 16 model sit at $92.00 while today's model lands at $74.00?

Three concrete adjustments explain the entire $18 gap: lowering Software's target multiple from 4.25x to 3.60x to reflect flat Arc Suite and Workiva's R&D lead (-$11 per share), incorporating $23.3 million of residual frozen pension liabilities plus slower Q3 buyback pace (-$4 per share), and trimming CCM EBITDA from $95 million to $88 million to reflect SEC e-delivery risk (-$3 per share). When every adjustment comes straight from audited 10-Q footnotes and competitor filings, lowering the target is intellectual honesty in action.

book_subsections.title: 7F. Capital Intensity, Goodwill Overhang, and True Return on Equity
paragraphs: Before leaving valuation, step back and inspect the quality of DFIN's balance sheet relative to its 3.86x Price-to-Book ratio. On the surface, 18.25% ROIC and 23.41% ROE look like classic asset-light software economics. Look at the September 30, 2026 balance sheet, however, and you find $405.5 million of goodwill sitting on $409.1 million of stockholders' equity—meaning 99.1% of book equity consists of historical acquisition goodwill, with 62.3% ($252.6 million) housed inside the cyclical Capital Markets CCM segment.

At the same time, DFIN carries $156.7 million in net receivables, including $22.8 million of unbilled revenue, net of a $21.5 million expected credit-loss reserve that absorbed $8.7 million in new provisions and $8.1 million in write-offs during the first nine months of 2026. Add $127.0 million of floating-rate SOFR debt maturing in March 2030 whose quarterly amortization doubles from 1.25% to 2.50% in 2028, and you see why investors demand a discount to pure-play cloud software multiples. Paying 7.46x EV-to-EBITDA is fair, not a mispriced bargain, until Software margins expand and goodwill risk shrinks.

book_subsections.title: 7G. What Separates a Value Trap From a Compounding Re-Rating
paragraphs: Many investors get burned in mid-cap transitions because they confuse a low trailing P/E ratio with a catalyst for multiple expansion. DFIN trades at 11.43x forward earnings today for one clear reason: consolidated top-line growth sits near 3% to 5%, while legacy Compliance and Communications Management still brings in almost half of revenue. Whenever legacy print runoff accelerates or IPO pipelines stall, consolidated growth stalls with it.

To break out of that valuation box permanently, DFIN needs Software Solutions to clear 55% to 60% of revenue without sacrificing segment profitability. Seeing CM-SS Adjusted EBITDA margin slip 490 basis points to 30.0% in Q3 2026 while legacy CM-CCM earned more quarterly EBITDA ($25.2 million vs. $19.2 million) proves the transition still faces growing pains. Until software margins expand and Arc Suite returns to growth, a $74.00 Base Fair Value accurately reflects both the cash flow strengths and the structural ceiling.

book_subsections.title: 7H. Walking Through the Exact Valuation Bridge From Q3 Cash Flow to Per-Share Value
paragraphs: Let's trace the exact bridge from Q3 2026 cash flow to our $74.00 per-share target so every listener can verify the math step by step. In the first nine months of 2026, DFIN generated $167.3 million in operating cash flow and $131.0 million in free cash flow, pushing trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA to $253.1 million. Management guided Q4 2026 revenue to $175 million to $180 million with 26% to 27% Adjusted EBITDA margin, implying full-year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA near $254 million.

When we look forward to FY2027, subtracting $34.3 million in annualized stock-based compensation from $247 million of consolidated Adjusted EBITDA yields roughly $212.7 million of economic EBITDA before capital spending. Applying a blended enterprise value of $1,811 million—derived from 3.60x Software sales ($1,458 million) plus 4.75x CCM EBITDA ($418 million) less $65 million corporate drag—equates to roughly 8.5x economic EBITDA, which is fair for a 3% to 5% top-line grower facing SEC e-delivery risk.

Finally, subtract $50 million for projected net debt and residual $23.3 million frozen pension obligations after eighteen months of free cash flow paydown, leaving $1,761 million of equity value. Divide by 23.8 million diluted shares—reflecting Q3's sharp slowdown in buybacks—and you arrive cleanly at $74.00 per share.

book_subsections.title: 7I. What Happens If Print Runoff Accelerates Under SEC E-Delivery?
paragraphs: One risk that conventional multiples overlook is the velocity of legacy print decay. In trailing twelve months, Print and Distribution generated $109.4 million, and IC-CCM generated $87.8 million across the first nine months of 2026. If the SEC's cross-divisional rulemaking project replaces paper-by-default rules with electronic delivery, physical mailing volumes could drop 10% to 15% per year instead of 4% to 5%.

At a 24% CCM EBITDA margin, losing $45 million of annual print revenue would trim roughly $10 million to $12 million from CCM EBITDA—reducing that segment's value by $50 million to $60 million, or more than $2.00 per share, even before accounting for potential Form N-PORT software softness. That asymmetric regulatory headwind is another reason why DFIN cannot command a pure-play SaaS multiple until print shrinks below 10% of total revenue.
